bare_s1.explanation: The unit responds mainly to the chin, throat and upper-chest area just below a dog's face (often including an open mouth or tongue). It responds somewhat more weakly to the same region on similar animals such as wolves, a ferret, a monkey and even a bird.

bare_s2.explanation: The unit responds to the throat, chin and upper chest just below the muzzle of dogs and wolves, often including an open mouth or tongue. It responds more weakly to the same neck region on other furry animals and birds.

Q0_s1.explanation: The unit responds to the throat/chest/lower-muzzle region of animals, mostly dogs and wolves, and also fires on other furry or feathered animals' necks.

Q0_s2.explanation: The unit responds to the throat, chest and lower-muzzle area of dogs and wolves, including open mouths with tongues. It also fires, nearly as strongly, on the same neck and chest region of other animals such as a bird, a ferret and a monkey.

F1_s1.explanation: The unit responds to the area just below a forward-facing head where a soft, finely fibrous surface curves into a broader body mass, often with a lighter patch or a small pink protruding shape beneath the jaw line. The response is strongest when the region is lit, mid-frame and fills a moderate part of the image.

F1_s2.explanation: The unit responds to the narrow region just below a forward-pointing head shape, where a face meets a neck or chest, especially when the surface there has fine, soft, hair-like texture. It responds more weakly to a glossy pink lobe hanging from an open mouth-like opening and to finely streaked versions of the same neck-region texture.

wrong.explanation: The unit responds broadly to man-made, often handcrafted or decorated objects such as fabric items, ornaments, accessories and gear. It may be keyed to curved, bordered or seamed contours, or to ornamental patterns on those objects, but no single concept is clear.
